articles.content_orig:
The Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, has said.
Marles said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” would be reviewed, but claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend.
The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong.
The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed.
“We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday.
“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts.
“Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained one of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology.
The US Department of War and F-35 Joint Program Office confirmed they were aware of the “shipment issue”.
“We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the spokesperson said.
While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them.
Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do.
“This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said.
Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, despite reported concerns from the US intelligence organisations that China could obtain some of the stealth technology.
Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries.
More than 70 Australian companies have production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” are manufactured in Victoria alone, according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales.
Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025.
Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries.
“They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the aircraft,” he said.
“So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F-35 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.”

Geoff Bennett: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington this evening for his first state visit in more than a decade. And at the same time, a federal judge today heard arguments in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico challenging President Trump banning them from the White House. Our Liz Landers is at the White House covering both stories, and she joins us now. So, Liz, we will start with this state visit. What is the focus of it? Liz Landers: Yes, Geoff, President Trump is greeting leader Xi right now at Joint Base Andrews here in Washington for an arrival ceremony that has all the pomp and circumstance of this major state visit. This is the first time that Xi has been to the White House since 2015. And President Trump visited China back in May and was not awarded this same kind of pomp, circumstance and arrival. In particular, Xi did not greet him when he landed there in China back in May. You're seeing some of those images now. I will remind our viewers that those images are from several months ago because the White House TV pool is still not covering the president's events today. We believe that there are going to be a number of issues that will be addressed during this visit. A senior administration official told us earlier that AI, artificial intelligence, of course, will be on the top of the list, also some of these export controls that the United States has on our computing chips and selling those to China. The possibility of reducing tariffs on some goods is apparently going to come up, and also political prisoners. Several China watchers and experts that I have spoken with don't really think that this meeting is going to be so much about deliverables as it is about continuing to forge that personal relationship that President Trump has with leader Xi. I spoke earlier today with Kyle Chan. He's a fellow at the Brookings institute. And he was actually talking about these export controls, saying that matters less and less for the Chinese government because they are going all out to build their own AI chips themselves. And when it comes to artificial intelligence in particular, you heard some of that addressed from the U.N. today in Nick's story. China is not interested in a joint slowdown of AI development, according to Chan. He says that they're more worried about cyber risks, hacking companies, and they don't share, China does not share the same concerns that we have heard from U.S. AI companies and leaders recently that robots, AI may kill us all in the near future. Geoff, one more thing I want to add. Not everybody is happy about this visit and all of the accoutrements that are being laid out for President Xi. Republican Senator Wicker, he's the chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, says that he would have advised against this lavish welcome to what he calls a brutal dictator. Geoff Bennett: And, Liz, there's a state dinner tomorrow evening. Who is expected to be in attendance? Liz Landers: Well, Geoff, as you would imagine, with all of this talk of AI and technology, there are leaders from several major business companies and AI companies that are going to be at the White House tomorrow. A senior administration official says that Jeff Bezos will be there, as well as Elon Musk, Michael Dell, Jensen Huang of Nvidia, a chipmaker, and Sam Altman of OpenAI. The first lady, Melania Trump, said in a FOX News interview today that President Trump wanted to have the state dinner because they have a great relationship. She said that she's been involved in every detail of the planning for the state dinner tomorrow night. And she also -- and I'd also just add that this is only the second state dinner that President Trump has now had in his second term in office, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: All right, Liz, in the minute we have left, bring us up to speed on this lawsuit involving the three news organizations that were banned from the White House by President Trump. It sounds like the judge believes that the due process of these news organizations was violated. The government is arguing in a filing that they issued late last night that news organizations failed to maintain basic minimum standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House. This has now turned into a conversation about national security. That is what the president and the administration are arguing is at stake here, that these news organizations somehow violated national security there. The judge also seemed skeptical of that, Geoff. We still do not have an answer from the judge as to whether the ban on Politico, CNN, and MS NOW will be lifted. Geoff Bennett: Liz Landers outside the West Wing at the White House for us tonight. Liz, thanks so much. Liz Landers: Of course.

Trump welcomes Xi to Washington as US, China agree to extend trade truce
Trump takes rare step of meeting foreign leader at the airport, underscoring the significance of US-China relationship.
China’s Xi visits US as Trump bets on stabilising global relations
United States President Donald Trump has welcomed his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to Washington, DC, for a three-day visit and high-stakes talks on trade, Taiwan and artificial intelligence.
Xi’s landed at Joint Base Andrews, outside the US capital, on Wednesday as the Trump administration announced that the two countries have agreed to extend an 11-month trade deal that offered temporary relief from punishing tariffs.
- list 1 of 3As Xi meets Trump, who’s winning their trade war?
- list 2 of 3What’s the US–China AI ‘hotline’ that Trump plans to pitch to Xi Jinping?
- list 3 of 3As AI leaders warn of catastrophe, US and China shun slowdown calls
Trump took the rare step of personally meeting Xi on his arrival, marking the first time in 11 years that a US president has greeted a foreign leader at the base, according to US media.
At the arrival ceremony, the leaders and their wives shook hands, spoke for a few minutes and stood for pictures as a military band played, cannons blasted and a B-1 military bomber flew overhead.
In a written statement afterwards, Xi said China and the US should be partners and not rivals, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. “He said that the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand, complement each other and benefit the world,” Xinhua reported.
Trump’s in-person greeting signals the significance that Washington ascribes to its relationship with Beijing, whose meteoric economic rise over the last several decades has transformed it into a global superpower capable of rivalling the US.
Xi’s visit comes after he hosted Trump in Beijing in May.
His schedule in Washington, DC, will include a state dinner attended by leaders of the US’s powerful tech industry, a military ceremony at the White House and a visit to the National Archives, home to documents of historical and cultural significance such as the US Constitution and the Declaration of Independence.
His talks with Trump are likely to cover the US-Israel war on Iran, the US-China trade deal, AI, and US ties to Taiwan, the self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, according to analysts.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Wednesday that he had met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng ahead of Xi’s visit to “see if we could do a bigger deal as opposed to just a series of smaller things”.
“We have agreed today that we will extend what we call the Busan Agreement,” Bessent said.
The agreement, which was set to expire on November 10, has now been extended to January 10, he said.
Yun Sun, a senior fellow and director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, said the short extension suggests the two nations were planning a wider deal.
“The two sides indeed have a bigger scope of negotiation coming to their trade deals, and they need more time to negotiate the technicalities,” she told Al Jazeera, adding that the truce was expected to hold even before the trip began.
Sun called Xi’s visit to the US “unprecedented”, saying “there has never been any precedent in the history of US-China relations for the top two leaders of the two countries to visit each other within a single year”. She described the stabilisation of ties as “quite prominent and very impressive”, noting that only 12 months ago, the two countries were escalating tariffs and export controls against each other.
On Taiwan, Sun said Beijing’s main goal would be to prevent or stall a $14bn arms package that Congress approved earlier this year, but the Trump administration has been unwilling to advance.
She said she expected the most progress on AI, where the two governments could agree on ways to manage their dialogue.
“We know that the US has proposed a hotline mechanism for notification to each other when there is a significant security risk associated with AI that happens in their individual country,” she said. “We’ll have to see whether the two leaders are able to make progress on this important issue.”

Sept. 23 (UPI) -- U.S. President Donald Trump greeted President Xi Jinping of China on Wednesday evening as the Chinese leader arrived at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, marking the start of a three-day state visit.
The tarmac greeting was a rare gesture for an incumbent U.S. president to a foreign leader. Trump and first lady Melania Trump met Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on a red carpet as the U.S. Air Force band performed the countries' national anthems. The ceremony also included a cannon salute, a 21-person honor cordon, color guards and a flyover by two B1 bombers.
There will be another ceremony Thursday morning at the White House featuring more than 500 U.S. service members. The presidents will meet Thursday afternoon with a state dinner Thursday night.
Both Republicans and Democrats have criticized the visit and the lavishness of Trump's treatment of the Chinese leader, The Hill reported . Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said onthe Senate floor Tuesday that Trump should remember that Xi "is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America."
A statement by a group of Senate Democrats including Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Chris Coons, D-Del., also criticized Trump's red-carpet treatment of the Chinese leader.
"President Xi gets the royal treatment while President Trump hurls threats and wages trade wars on allies like Canada," they wrote. "This is not leadership, and Americans deserve better."
The Democrats called on Trump to end China's access "to the advanced chips and manufacturing equipment it needs to build dangerous AI systems," stand with Taiwan against China and press Xi to stop supporting Russia's war in Ukraine.
The trip marks XI's first state visit to the United States in 11 years.

articles.title_zh: U.S.-China trade truce extended for two months, Bessent says, as Xi begins state visit
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. and China have extended a truce to keep tariffs lower for longer and rare earths flowing, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday local time.
He was speaking on Fox News, as Chinese President Xi Jinping landed in Washington, D.C. for a state visit through Friday.
Xi and Trump agreed to a one-year trade truce at a meeting in South Korea last October. The deal, which was set to expire in November, will now be extended to Jan. 10, Bessent said. He added that Beijing needs to fulfill more deliverables.
Ahead of this week's summit, many had expected the truce would be extended by six months or longer.
Chinese state media did not immediately note Bessent's comments on the trade truce.
The two-month extension "suggests to me the U.S. is unsatisfied with China's offers and wants to keep the heat on, with a bonus being it is more likely that Xi goes to the G20 in Miami," said Scott Kennedy of the U.S.-based think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Trump visited Beijing in May. The two leaders could also meet alongside an APEC meeting in Shenzhen in November, and the G20 summit in Miami in December.
However, Jens Eskelund, president of the European Chamber of Commerce in China, pointed out that simply extending the trade truce does not address challenges companies face, including the lack of a standardized approach to apply for rare earths export licenses.
Xi said in an official readout for his arrival that he is confident the visit will produce "fruitful results" for both sides. He said the two countries should be partners, not rivals, and work to build a stable relationship where competition and differences are managed. The readout did not mention tariffs, rare earths or artificial intelligence.
Footage streamed on China's state broadcaster showed U.S. President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump meeting Xi and First Lady of China Peng Liyuan at the foot of the Chinese leader's jet. The video did not show the U.S. and Chinese leaders shaking hands — it focused on Xi and his wife shaking hands with two children presenting them each with bouquets.
After greeting Xi, Trump told reporters he would discuss the Iran war with the Chinese leader, among "many other subjects."
Bessent met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York ahead of Xi's arrival in the U.S. The two sides discussed setting up an alert system for AI incidents, according to Bessent.
While executives of major U.S. tech companies plan to join a summit dinner on Thursday, none of their Chinese counterparts are expected to attend.
Politburo Standing Committee Member Cai Qi and China's top diplomat Wang Yi accompanied Xi, according to state media.
—CNBC's Eunice Yoon and Ashlee Trujillo contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Meta is trying VR glasses (again), this time with more IMAX
articles.title_zh: Meta is trying VR glasses (again), this time with more IMAX
articles.content_orig:
Meta is renewing its quest to make virtual reality a thing. At its Connect event on Wednesday, the company announced Meta VR Glasses, its newest entry into the VR market, which will be available next spring starting at $1,299.99.
These glasses actually seem quite promising, thanks to a substantially lighter form factor and a host of new entertainment integrations — including (allegedly) IMAX compatibility.
Moments before unveiling them, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg reminded the audience that the company had decided awhile ago to shift its focus away from the Metaverse and build fewer VR devices until it had real breakthroughs.
“This is a breakthrough,” he exclaimed before showing off the glasses. “A lot of people agree that augmented reality glasses with holograms are clearly going to be part of the future, but we’ve also heard that a lot of people are less interested in wearing a headset. So we have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion with high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time.”
Meta says that the glasses are five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3 — and they look much more like normal eyewear than the bulky headsets the company has released before. The frames are made of magnesium alloy, and the glasses are powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite processor. They connect to a computing puck that doubles as a battery, which users can just slip the puck into their pocket to use the glasses on the go.
The glasses are largely built for entertainment. Micro-OLED panels built into the lenses provide what Meta calls a 5K Infinite Display with 37 pixels per degree, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos audio support. Users will be able to download and watch movies.
Perhaps one of the more unique features of the glasses, however, is that Meta is pitching them as a great way to enjoy IMAX-captured films.
Indeed, the company calls the glasses the “first IMAX-enhanced certified VR device ever” and says they will be one of the few ways to experience the expanded aspect ratio that defines IMAX’s distinct high-resolution viewing experience.
The glasses also support 3D content, including movies that integrate a user’s physical space into their viewing experience. Meta says that it has teamed up with Disney and that in November, Disney+ users will be able to stream specific movies — including certain Marvel movies — in 3D.
Meta says that users will be able to watch specific movies and have their surroundings “transformed with immersive environments, dynamic effects, stunning 3D visuals, and spatial audio” — essentially converting the movie into a VR gaming-type experience.
The glasses will also come with Meta AI — its automated virtual assistant — built in, which means that users will be able to talk to the glasses and automate various tasks via voice command. For instance, Meta says you’ll be able to start a movie just by asking your glasses to do so. Other ways to issue commands include hand gestures.

articles.title_orig: Meta VR Glasses Officially Announced, Shipping Spring 2027 For $1300
articles.title_zh: Meta VR Glasses Officially Announced, Shipping Spring 2027 For $1300
articles.content_orig:
Meta VR Glasses were just officially announced. Priced at $1300, they have 2.4K micro-OLED displays, weigh 100 grams, and are powered by a tethered puck with Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset.
The puck runs the same operating system as Quest 3, and supports all the same content, rendered at notably higher resolution thanks to a combination of the more powerful chipset (essentially an XR2 Gen 3 by a different name) and eye-tracked foveated rendering. It features 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage, and there's a microSD slot in the puck to expand it.
The caveat to the content compatibility is that Meta VR Glasses do not come with controllers by default, but you can buy Touch Plus controllers separately (available in a new all-black color), or pair the controllers from your existing Quest 3 or Quest 3S, and there'll be a bundle with controllers "in some retail channels".
The stark difference between Meta VR Glasses and any Quest, however, is the split architecture, and the dramatic reduction in weight and bulk this enables.
Meta VR Glasses have no onboard computing, not even a tracking coprocessor, and thus entirely rely on the puck, which provides both power and data over a thin and flexible fiber optic cable.
The visor has an open-periphery design, so you naturally see the real world to your sides and below you. It's built with a magnesium alloy that minimizes weight while also enabling a fanless, passively cooled design that weighs "around" 100 grams.
Another key difference is the display and field of view. With dual 120Hz 2412×2288 HDR micro-OLED displays, Meta VR Glasses have the highest resolution of any Meta headset to date, and are the company's first non-LCD headset since the original Oculus Quest.
The displays support the Dolby Vision HDR format, Meta says it's the first VR device to be IMAX Enhanced certified.
The form factor brings a major optical compromise, though: the field of view. Meta advertises 70° horizontal × 66° vertical (equating to 87° diagonal) compared to the roughly 110° horizontal × 96° vertical of Quest 3.
The lower field of view will make Meta VR Glasses feel far less immersive than a Quest headset when the optional light blockers are attached for fully immersive experiences. But, somewhat ironically given the name of the product, Meta VR Glasses should shine without the light blockers in passthrough mixed reality, where a natural view of your periphery is arguably preferable to darkness.
Meta plans to market the product as "a private cinema, multiple virtual monitor workspace, and game console in one device that fits in your bag".
Essentially, Meta VR Glasses at its core is the same product proposition as the Xreal Aura Android XR glasses but with a VR-style passthrough display system that offers a larger field of view (87° diagonal vs Xreal's 70°), higher resolution, and full opacity, alongside the inclusion of eye tracking and optional tracked controllers. We do not yet know the price of Xreal Aura.
To expand the library of content available to all Meta VR Glasses buyers, Meta announced a swathe of new hand tracking VR and mixed reality games, including a new hand-tracked Beat Saber mode called Flux. You can read about the gaming announcements here.
For the first time for a Meta standalone device, you can also plug in any USB-C DisplayPort device to the puck and have it shown as a huge virtual screen in Meta VR Glasses, without the need for a capture card.
Meta VR Glasses will also feature the first implementation of Hologram, the company's productization of its Codec Avatars research. Similar to Apple Vision Pro's Personas, it will let you join flatscreen WhatsApp video calls as a photorealistic face-tracked avatar, and appear as a realistic full-scale avatar for other Meta VR Glasses (and eventually Quest 3) owners.
However, at launch in spring, your spatial Hologram will be a "2.5D" stereoscopic video stream, at true scale but only seen as a front-angle view. Even if you change your perspective, the Hologram will stay as a head-on perspective. Meta says it plans to evolve Hologram over time to become a truly 6DoF 3D system, at which point it will become the default platform-level avatar experience for its VR platform, effectively superseding the cartoon Meta Avatars.

articles.title_orig: Meta Announces ‘VR Glasses’ Next-Gen XR Headset, Priced at $1,300
articles.title_zh: Meta Announces ‘VR Glasses’ Next-Gen XR Headset, Priced at $1,300
articles.content_orig:
Meta today unveiled its long-awaited next-gen mixed reality headset: Meta VR Glasses.
Previously known under the codename ‘Project Phoenix’, Meta VR Glasses was announced today, but isn’t launching just yet; the compute puck-tethered device is slated to go one sale sometime in Spring 2027, priced at $1,300.
While we’re still waiting on a precise release date, Meta did reveal an avalanche of details on the hardware alongside a slate of new immersive and casual viewing content coming to the headset. You can catch Road to VR’s hands-on with Meta VR Glasses here.
Meta VR Glasses – Hardware
Meta VR Glasses feature what the company is calling its ‘5K Infinite Display’, which uses micro-OLED panels, offering a 5.5MP (2,412 x 2,288) per-eye resolution at 37 pixels per degree (PPD)—notably higher than Quest 3’s 25 PPD.
In fact, despite being significant lower resolution than Vison Pro’s 11.7MP per-eye resolution, Meta says VR Glasses has a higher PPD (34 vs 37) because VR Glasses spreads its pixels over a tighter field-of-view of about 88° diagonally (H70° × V66°).
That’s not the only thing that’s smaller. Meta VR Glasses weigh about 100g on the head, as the battery and compute have been moved to a separate puck connected to a proprietary port via an optical cable.
Inside that pocketable puck (~300g) is Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor (XR2 Gen 3) and a battery with a claimed 3+ hours of mixed use. The puck can also be used charged while in use, when plugged into its included 45W USB-C power supply.
Lenses can be manually adjusted for a interpupillary distance (IPD) range between 56–70mm, and can also be fit with prescription inserts from Meta partner Zenni Optical.
As for sensors, VR Glasses comes with a wide array: eye-tracking cameras for UI selection and biometric unlock, front and downward-facing camera sensors for a wider hand-tracking range, and full color passthrough sensors offering 26 PPD. It of course also does the same capable 6DOF spatial tracking pioneered in the company’s Quest lineup.
Like its Meta Ray-Ban Display smart glasses, Meta VR Glasses support a mix of gaze and hand gestures: look to highlight a button, pinch your fingers together to select, rub your thumb up or down, or side to side to scroll through content.
While that mix of eye and hand-tracking is its main input scheme (i.e., not shipping with physical controllers), Meta VR Glasses do support Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, which the company says you can either buy separately or actually use from your existing Meta Quest 3 or 3S.
Meta is also baking in Surface Keyboard—released earlier this year on Quest—to turn any flat surface into a keyboard and trackpad, which comes in addition to being able to pair Bluetooth peripherals like keyboards, gamepads, and more.
Meta VR Glasses are being offered in two sizes (for different head sizes), Standard and Large, which are notably two separate SKUs. Only one storage option has been announced thus far: 128GB internal storage with the option to expand up to 1TB via the puck’s microSD card slot.
When they do launch next spring, Meta VR Glasses are targeting broad international availability, with supported regions including: US, UK, Canada, Mexico, Germany, Poland, France, Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, Switzerland, Austria, Ireland, Iceland, Finland, Spain, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Japan, Taiwan, Korea, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand.
Meta VR Glasses – Software & Games
Meta VR Glasses run the same OS and store as Quest, so the entire Quest catalog of VR games and apps are there.
At least in terms of gaming without Touch controllers, Meta has promised 75+ games and apps optimized for hand gesture input, with its headliners including a modified version of Beat Saber for hand-tracking, 3D puzzle game Dragon Grove, courtroom sim Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney, Dual Destinies, and a modified version of Tetris Effect for hand-tracking.
Meta says all of your usual streaming apps will be there at launch: Disney+ and Peacock, both with 3D, plus HBO, YouTube, Prime Video and more. Other streaming services can also be accessed via the built-in browser.
Meta VR Glasses is also technically an ‘IMAX Enhanced’ certified VR device supporting Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos immersive spatial audio, which means you’ll be able to watch select films in IMAX’s exclusive expanded aspect ratio.
Outside of casual gaming, video, and 180-degree immersive sports content, which you also find on Quest, Meta is leaning particularly hard into productivity.
The device supports wireless multi-screen virtual desktop streaming from Mac, PC or phone, opening it up to be more of a general computing device. Native DisplayPort-In also allows you to directly wire into laptops, consoles and handhelds.

articles.title_orig: US, China agree to extend trade truce by two months, work on bigger deal, Bessent says
articles.title_zh: US, China agree to extend trade truce by two months, work on bigger deal, Bessent says
articles.content_orig:
The United States and China have agreed to extend a bilateral trade truce that was set to expire in November through Jan. 10, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday.
The announcement came after Bessent and China’s vice premier, He Lifeng, held an unscheduled meeting in Washington.
“We will extend what we call the ‘Busan Agreement’ — the economic détente between the two countries that was scheduled to end on Nov. 10 — that is going to be extended until Jan. 10,” Bessent said in an interview on Fox News Channel.
Bessent said it’s possible a larger economic package will be agreed upon by January. But it’s also possible to “just roll the current deal” and extend it further.
Trump welcomes Xi at Joint Base Andrews
“There are some deliverables that have not been perfect on the Chinese side, so we also want to see, now that we’ve sat down and told them our expectations, if over the coming months they can be more fulsome in enacting the agreement,” he said.
The announcement, a big win for economic stability in both countries, came only minutes after Chinese President Xi Jinping touched down to begin a multiday state visit to Washington.
Bessent also indicated that there could be further announcements in coming days from the Chinese delegation, including agreements to buy more American agricultural products and potential deals in the financial services sector.
Since Sunday, Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have been holding talks with their Chinese counterparts to lay the groundwork for the closely watched state visit.
On Sunday, Bessent and Greer announced that the U.S. and China had proposed exchanging alerts about AI-related hacking incidents, especially those that concern national security.
The U.S. and China could also agree on lists of goods on which lower tariffs would be applied as part of President Donald Trump’s “Board of Trade” initiative with China, Greer told reporters.
“We expect that the types of goods you’ll see in those lists are consumer goods, low-tech items coming in from the Chinese side,” he said. “On the U.S. side, energy products, agricultural goods, potentially medical devices and other things like that.”
Xi’s trip is his first state visit to the U.S. in more than a decade.
News of the trade truce extension is likely to be widely welcomed in Washington and Beijing, given that the U.S. and China are vital sources of goods for each other and for their millions of consumers and businesses.

articles.title_orig: Trump greets China’s Xi at airport in historic move — as nations agree to trade truce to kick off high-stakes DC visit
articles.title_zh: Trump greets China’s Xi at airport in historic move — as nations agree to trade truce to kick off high-stakes DC visit
articles.content_orig:
Trump greets China’s Xi at airport in historic move — as nations agree to trade truce to kick off high-stakes DC visit
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Add The New York Post on Google
WASHINGTON — President Trump personally welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the US on Wednesday evening — as the nations kicked off a three-day state visit by announcing a trade truce lasting through Jan. 10.
Trump, joined by first lady Melania Trump, made the unusual decision to greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews — a gesture not made by Xi when Trump visited Beijing in May.
The last time an American president greeted a world leader at JBA was in 1962 when John F. Kennedy met British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan.
Trump stood at the bottom of the steps to Xi’s plane and shook his hand before escorting him down a red carpet — with a B-1 Lancer bomber making a flyover as the American national anthem played.
Six F-16s and six F-22s were lined up on the tarmac, showcasing US military might.
Trump told reporters as he returned to the White House that it was “a great greeting, and I think they appreciate it — tremendous people.”
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, meanwhile, appeared on Fox News to announce that the US and China agreed not to escalate tariffs until at least 2027.
“We will extend what we call the ‘Busan Agreement,’ the economic detente between the two countries that was scheduled to end on Nov. 10 — that is going to be extended until Jan. 10,” Bessent said.
“There are some deliverables that have not been perfect on the Chinese side, so we also want to see, now that we’ve sat down and told them our expectations.”
Xi’s visit is expected to touch on a wide range of tensions in the US-China relationship, including tariffs, fentanyl exports, artificial intelligence and Beijing’s role in conflicts ranging from Iran to Ukraine.
Trump has repeatedly said he believes a strong personal relationship between the leaders can notch benefits for the American people, though it’s unclear what concrete agreements may come.
Xi will be treated to a state dinner at the White House on Thursday — with the US leader likely to show off his recent renovations, including a new granite helipad with the presidential seal and an enormous ballroom with concrete walls now protruding from the site of the former East Wing.
The relationship between Trump and Xi has had ups and downs, featuring warm in-person greetings but souring during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and during last year’s US-China trade war.
Trump, seeking to force a new trade deal that rebalances the US trade deficit and to punish China’s export of illicit fentanyl, ramped up tariffs on China last year, and Xi retaliated in kind.
The trade clash saw US tariffs on Chinese goods near 150% — before a cooling off following a meeting last October meeting between Trump and Xi in South Korea, where Xi agreed to do more to quash fentanyl exports that killed about 488,000 Americans over the past decade, peaking in 2022 and 2023.
China threatened during the tit-for-tat ramp-up to impose restrictions on rare earth materials, and the US stopped advanced chip sales that Beijing could use to give it a key boost in the artificial intelligence race.
A senior US official told reporters ahead of Xi’s visit that the Trump administration is dissatisfied with Xi’s actions to reduce fentanyl smuggling.
“It does not appear that China has elevated this issue,” the official said. “China is the overwhelming, predominant supplier of precursor chemicals to the cartels in Mexico and remains so. And they have done a number of anecdotal things, including a few arrests recently, but we’d like to see much more systemic change.”
Fentanyl deaths — which Trump cited in his initial wave of tariffs last year — have dipped in the US, but remain elevated and factors such as the availability of test strips and overdose antidotes and improved border detection may have eased the impact. Still, about 35,000 Americans died in the past year.
Trump’s personal warmth with Xi has in the past been coupled with shows of American strength — with the president often recounting a 2017 visit by Xi to Mar-a-Lago. The men were enjoying dessert as Trump revealed that the US had just conducted airstrikes on Syria.
“We had the most beautiful piece of chocolate cake that you’ve ever seen, and President Xi was enjoying it,” Trump remembered afterward. “He was eating his cake. And he was silent.”

articles.title_zh: New Details Emerge About ICE Officer Who Shot Man in Austin
articles.content_orig:
US judge blocks deportation of DoorDash driver shot by ICE
A US judge has temporarily blocked the deportation of a Venezuelan man who was shot by immigration agents in Texas, his lawyer says.
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, is being held in a detention centre with a bullet in his back, according to his lawyer. Judge Orlando Garcia, a Clinton appointee, scheduled a hearing for Garces Perez to appear in court in person next week.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement that an "illegal alien" had been the subject of a targeted vehicle stop but pushed back against suggestions he had been given inadequate medical care.
The incident comes months after a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man in Houston.
Garces Perez's immigration lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, has filed a federal lawsuit for a temporary restraining order to prevent his removal from the country.
Since the judge ordered that her client appear in person on 30 September, he cannot be deported before then, she said.
"For now, we have secured a temporary block on his deportation while his case moves forward," Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote on social media.
"This is an important step, but our work is not over," she wrote. "Wilber still needs appropriate medical care, and we will continue fighting to protect his rights."
The gunshot fractured his clavicle and he is wearing a sling while having "significant swelling and pain," Lincoln-Goldfinch said.
The cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced has not yet been determined, she said.
A spokesperson for US Attorney's Office in Texas declined to comment on the case.
The ICE agent who shot him - who joined the agency last year - was not wearing a body camera at the time of the shooting, sources told the BBC’s US partner CBS News.
The Austin Police Department released footage from officers responding to the scene, but did not show what led to the incident.
On Tuesday, DHS pushed back against what it called "false narratives" surrounding what had happened, blaming sanctuary cities and media for "spreading lies" and discouraging people from resisting officers and evading arrest.
"Contrary to their claims, this person is an illegal alien who has no legal status to be here and has been given some of the best medical care he's ever received in his life," said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in a statement to the BBC.
DHS said the man, whom they did not name, was "the subject of a targeted vehicle stop" and that his work permit expired last year.
"No amount of smears and false narratives will slow down ICE from doing its job by removing dangerous illegal aliens from our communities and making America safe again," Mullin said.
The Austin Police Department, which was not involved in the incident, released dashcam and body camera footage on Tuesday showing its officers at the scene.
It does not show the shooting, but several gunshots can be heard in one dashcam clip, while another shows officers approaching Garces Perez's car and detaining him. At one point, Garces Perez's t-shirt is cut to reveal what appears to be a single gunshot in his back.
Lincoln-Goldfinch previously told the BBC that after being unable to move his arm in the detention facility, Garces Perez was taken back to hospital on Monday evening. He was treated there and has since been returned to the detention facility.
He said he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly during his transfer, despite his injury, she said.
Lincoln-Goldfinch added that detention personnel had revoked his communication privileges and moved him from an infirmary into an isolated room with a flat, non-adjustable bed.
In its statement on Tuesday, DHS said Garces Perez had received medical care "around the clock" and denied claims he received no pain medication and was forced to sleep on the floor.
"This alien was released from the hospital and arrived at the detention facility just a few hours later, where he slept on a bed," DHS said.
Texas lawmaker Joaquin Castro, a Democrat, on Tuesday demanded the Venezuelan national's release from detention.
Local and state officials have pushed for an independent investigation into the shooting, which occurred just before on Sunday afternoon.
Hours later, dozens of protesters, some waving the flags of Mexico and Guatemala, gathered at the scene carrying signs demanding that ICE leave the city.
DHS said on Tuesday that ICE "will not be slowing down nor leaving Austin".
The man's lawyer told US media he was making a DoorDash delivery when an unmarked black truck sideswiped his car.
He did not know the truck was an ICE vehicle and made a U-turn, she said. His car was hit again before agents got out and shot him, according to the attorney.

articles.content_orig:
• All eyes on Venezuela: The country’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez addressed the UN General Assembly more than eight months after the US captured her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro. She said Venezuela will hold elections and transition to a full democracy — but didn’t specify when — and thanked US President Donald Trump for his “readiness” toward diplomacy.
• Iran president speaks: Earlier, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran will not bend to Trump and asserted Iranians have been “the victims of terrorism.” A US delegate in the room walked out.
• No breakthrough: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said US-Iran mediated talks on the sidelines of the UN did not yield any major breakthrough, indicating the memorandum of understanding from earlier this year was no longer in the cards.
• Zelensky delivers remarks: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called Vladimir Putin “patient zero,” saying the Russian leader spreads war and instability. As he spoke, Zelensky’s party headquarters were struck by Russia, according to Kyiv officials.
Delcy Rodríguez thanks Trump for "willingness to resume the path of diplomatic relations"
Venezuela’s acting president Delcy Rodríguez thanked President Donald Trump this evening for what she called “his willingness to resume the path of diplomatic relations and cooperation” with her country.
During her debut address to the United Nations General Assembly, Rodríguez said Venezuela seeks to “be reborn” following two blows suffered this year: first, the “strangulation of its internal political life and the heightened confrontation with the United States”; and second, the double earthquakes of June 24.
The earthquakes were devastating toVenezuela, causing the deaths of more than 6,500 people and extensive material damage.
Venezuela to hold elections, transition to democracy, acting president tells UNGA
Venezuela will hold elections and transition to a full democracy, acting President Delcy Rodríguez said Wednesday at the UN General Assembly.
Rodríguez didn’t specify when a vote will be held, only saying that the Venezuelan people will “determine when the correct time for these elections is.”
Rodríguez, who became acting president after the United States toppled strongman leader Nicolás Maduro, said the democratic transition is underway and promised that the process would be transparent, inclusive and verifiable.
“We have begun a political dialogue with sectors of the opposition, which will lead to a process where everyone will compete on an equal footing,” she said.
Rodriguez delivered her speech a day after Venezuela’s exiled opposition leader María Corina Machado attempted to return to the country but was denied entry three times, according to her advisers.
European Council president meets Iran’s Pezeshkian on UNGA sidelines
European Council President Antonio Costa met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly and called on Iran to cease strikes on its neighbors.
Costa said the two leaders had a “frank and substantial discussion,” and urged Iran to restore freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, which has been a major point of contention in the Iran war.
“I stressed that dialogue is the only way to resolve conflicts and to ensure lasting peace across the region,” Costa posted to X.
Costa also urged Iran to resume cooperation with the UN nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Iran has said it will not comply with demands from the agency to inspect its bombed nuclear sites, citing the absence of established regulations for inspecting facilities damaged by military strikes.
In June, Israel and the United States carried out significant military strikes targeting Iran’s nuclear program, damaging key sites including Natanz, Fordow, and Isfahan.
How Venezuela's Delcy Rodríguez faced her worst crisis yet after devastating earthquakes
The devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela in late June would have tested any government. But they hit a country still navigating the aftermath of strongman Nicolás Maduro’s capture nearly 10 months ago, turning a natural disaster into a political test for acting President Delcy Rodríguez and exposing anger over the state’s response.
The two catastrophic earthquakes that struck in quick succession on June 24 have left more than 6,500 dead, according to figures released in late August by the President of the National Assembly of Venezuela, Jorge Rodríguez.
Both inside and outside the country, many citizens claimed authorities responded too slowly and failed to adequately address the tragedy, a criticism Rodríguez firmly rejects.
Analysts interviewed by CNN say the earthquakes have become a defining test for the interim government, exposing its political vulnerability and the limits of the state’s power to respond to the disaster. They argue that its outcome remains highly uncertain and that the actions of the United States will be decisive, given the supervisory role Washington currently plays in Venezuela.
The June 24 earthquakes rank among the deadliest natural disasters in Venezuela’s history.
A disaster of this magnitude would challenge any government, but analysts argue that Venezuela’s situation is particularly severe because it occurred in a country with institutions weakened by 25 years of rule by followers of the late President Hugo Chávez.
The US-Venezuela deal to control 65 billion barrels of oil reserves
President Donald Trump announced last month that the United States had reached an oil agreement with Venezuela, a move he said will “more than double” American oil reserves, increase oil supply and lower gas prices.
What this means: Under the agreement, the Pentagon’s little-known Office of Strategic Capital will acquire up to a 35% equity stake in a company that owns North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), the second-largest private oil producer in Venezuela.
NABEP plans to invest $100 billion in new infrastructure to produce oil from its fields, according to the White House.
The company is controlled by the family of Alejandro Betancourt López, a controversial international businessman based in the UK. Betancourt has been investigated — but not yet charged — in Spain on fraud and money laundering charges, and a similar investigation closed in Switzerland without charges.
A spokesperson for NABEP did not respond to a request for comment. The White House said NABEP will be subject to US laws, and the US government will be able to veto any board member appointment.
In addition to the equity stake, the US State Department has the right to purchase 20% of the Venezuelan oil produced by NABEP at the cost of production. The State Department also has the right of first refusal to buy the rest of the proceeds.
In all, the Trump administration says the plan gives it a 55% stake in the new joint venture.
A look at the current state of US-Venezuela relations
On January 3, US forces undertook a high-stakes operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro from a compound in Caracas and transport him to the US to face criminal charges.
Maduro’s vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, assumed the position of acting president. Since then, Rodríguez, a stalwart of both the Hugo Chávez and Maduro governments, has worked to win US President Donald Trump’s support while keeping Chavismo alive.
Rodríguez, who is speaking today at the UN General Assembly, has overseen tactical concessions to Washington, including favorable positions in strategic sectors like oil, and permitting increased US oversight and presence in the country. Meanwhile, much has stayed the same inside Venezuela under her rule, and little progress has been made toward holding democratic elections.
In August, the Venezuelan government met with opposition figures to begin US-backed talks aimed toward a democratic transition. On September 2, Trump said Venezuela is “not going to be ready” for democratic elections but looks forward to holding them

articles.title_orig: Judge skeptical of Trump's White House media ban at hearing
articles.title_zh: Judge skeptical of Trump's White House media ban at hearing

US Justice Dept says Trump can deny journalists White House access
CNN, MS NOW and Politico can be shut out from areas of the White House at President Donald Trump's request, the Department of Justice said on Tuesday, a day ahead of a court hearing.
The three leading outlets went to court after Trump ordered on Friday that they be barred from the presidential mansion as punishment for distributing what he calls "fake news."
A US district judge set a hearing on the complaint for Wednesday.
The Department of Justice said in a court filing that Trump can "control reporters' access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office."
"Access to the White House is a privilege -- not a right," it added.
The court filing said that letters explaining the president's reasons for the ban had been sent to the outlets on Tuesday. They have until Friday to object.
The letters cite numerous "reporting incidents" by the outlets that "threatened national security and spread falsehoods," according to the filing.
The letter to CNN cited a story on Trump's plans to build a bunker below the East Wing ballroom he is constructing, which "disclosed 'top-secret' construction details," and several stories about the Iran war, the network said.
Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied any access to the White House grounds on Saturday and had their passes confiscated.
In their lawsuit, the three outlets asked for a temporary restraining order against the ban on the grounds that it violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press.
"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the outlets said in the court filing.
On Tuesday, Trump appeared to have suggested that CNN should not be covering him outside of the White House too.
"I'm surprised that CNN is here covering me, you shouldn't be here," Trump told reporters covering his visit to the United Nations General Assembly this week.
Trump has long attacked media outlets that have aired critical coverage of his campaigns and administrations, repeatedly blasting the press as the "enemy of the people."
But the ban comes at a time when his approval ratings are at record lows, his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in November's midterm elections, and the war in the Middle East drags on with no end in sight.

articles.title_orig: Future of Air Force’s China Aerospace Studies Institute uncertain
articles.title_zh: Future of Air Force’s China Aerospace Studies Institute uncertain
articles.content_orig:
The Department of the Air Force is shutting down its premier think tank dedicated to studying Chinese aerospace, despite previously saying it would only cut civilian roles, according to the organization’s director.
On Tuesday, an Air Force spokesperson told Federal News Network that the service would no longer assign civilian positions to the China Aerospace Studies Institute as a part of the ongoing civilian restructure within Air Education and Training Command.
The spokesperson, however, did not confirm the assertion that CASI is shutting down, saying instead that the “mission continues with the organization leveraging assigned military service members to accomplish its objectives.”
“The China Aerospace Studies Institute is not closing,” the spokesperson said. “Air University continues to evaluate the alignment of the CASI mission to best support DAF priorities.”
“Civilian employees affected by this restructure will continue in their current positions until further notice and will be evaluated for reassignment,” the spokesperson added.
CASI’s official X account later published a statement that “Air University has decided to close the China Aerospace Studies Institute.”
Brendan Mulvaney, the organization’s director, said that all of CASI’s billets will go into an unfunded status beginning Oct. 1.
“That doesn’t mean we are going to cease operations right on the first of October. CASI has commitments that it has made and will honor, to the best of our ability, through at least March of 2027,” Mulvaney, who has been the center’s director since 2017, said in a statement.
“What it does mean is that the amazing team of researchers and scholars at CASI are going to have to start to look for new positions elsewhere. Rest assured, CASI employees will continue to work and get paid while in a ‘surplus’ status (meaning they remain employed and paid while we help them find new positions), and I will do my best to make sure they all land someplace that will truly appreciate their talents… As time goes on, unless we find a new home within the Department for the whole CASI team, I expect people to find other jobs and move on. Once all of the civilians eventually depart, CASI will close,” he added.
The Air Force spokesperson said that eight civilian positions have been impacted by the service’s 2026 civilian workforce optimization effort.
“Employees filling those positions will continue to serve and support CASI alongside five military members for the foreseeable future,” the spokesperson said.
CASI opened its doors in 2017 to study China’s air and space capabilities. The organization’s unclassified research informs policy and strategy across the Defense Department and broader U.S. government.
The defense community called the Air Force’s decision to “shutter” CASI “extremely unfortunate and regrettable,” describing the center as “the most prolific producer of publicly-accessible open source research about [the People’s Liberation Army] in the United States.”
“CASI has measurably increased knowledge about the PLA within the U.S. government, academia, think tanks and the broader public, which should be in the U.S. government’s interest, given that strategic competition with the PRC is the most important,” Will Yale, a Navy surface warfare officer, said on social media platform X.
Ryan Fedasiuk, a fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, said it is a “truly incomprehensible decision and a devastating loss for the analytic community.”
Workforce cuts at CASI are part of the Defense Department’s ongoing efforts to restructure its civilian workforce — the department eliminated approximately 78,000 civilian positions in 2025.

Dolly Parton's family war is getting ugly ... with her longtime manager filing a lawsuit seeking a temporary restraining order against the late singer's nephew, Bryan Seaver, TMZ has learned.
TMZ obtained court docs filed by Dolly's manager, Danny Nozell. The manager claims Bryan began "invoking his self-proclaimed military-contractor experience, access to weapons, and capacity for violence" to extort Dolly's manager into giving in to his demands for money.
The manager said he was forced to terminate Bryan due to his threatening conduct ... and said he started a campaign of threats, intimidation, and coercion a few weeks before her passing.
One alleged threat read, "Her money better be bigger than I can make elsewhere or I'm going to f*** everyone. I am about to become the hand of retribution for my entire family."
Another alleged threat sent by Bryan read, "I’m going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnership and telling the violations these people have done on us."
Another alleged message read, "All I do is warfare ... everyone needs to be worried about what I might do." Seaver also allegedly wrote "I'm not an entertainment person. I'm a killer" and "I'm going to ratf**k every entity I can possibly conjure" in messages submitted as exhibits.
The manager terminated Bryan on September 15. His lawsuit is asking for Bryan to not interfere with Dolly's business and leave their business partners alone ... and stay 1,000 feet away from the offices.
As TMZ first reported, Seaver was recently kicked off her properties after working as her head of security for years.
Bryan denies the claims in the petition. He tells TMZ ... "I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer."
He added, "However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by." Bryan said the messages were taken out of context to make it look like he was threatening people.
"I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend and he fancies himself a gangster," he said. "A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."
In regard to the "rat f**k" comment, Bryan tells us "I was talking about people that have done bad to Dolly in business – a specific company that scared her and intimated her. Those comments were about specific, horrible business partners that have done wrong to her and I stand by that."
Dolly died on August 25, 2026, at the age of 80 ... and Bryan himself announced via her Instagram.

articles.title_orig: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
articles.title_zh: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
articles.content_orig:
Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table.
In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, his first since the US and Israel launched an all-out war on Iran, Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to the US.
But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk, saying: “It must be understood by President Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.”
On Tuesday, the US president had told the UN he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington’s negotiators.
A surprise three-hour meeting between Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the assembly the same day was regarded as constructive by both sides. It was the first such meeting since June, but did not stop the US delegation from walking out at the start of Pezeshkian’s speech.
The Iranian president did not go into any details about the talks, but conveyed the impression that he was focused on winning the support of Iran’s Arab neighbours for the proposals Tehran has drawn up for the future of the strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway that has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war, causing global energy prices to soar.
He made it clear Iran could not tolerate the strait being used to transport arms that could then be used against it, a statement that suggests the Islamic republic will demand the right to inspect ships travelling through the strait in the future. Iran’s goal, he said, was to live independently.
Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating the supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war. He held up photographs of the dead leader and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict, before insisting Tehran had never started a war.
“We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.”
He said Iran had the right to pursue a peaceful civil nuclear programme and it did not want to build nuclear weapons.
He repeatedly argued that the answer to regional security lay in agreement within the region and not with outsiders such as the US. Iran did not see its neighbours as security rivals, he said, but as partners in security. “In today’s world, those that are unable to defend themselves will be trampled upon,” he added.
Iran has repeatedly targeted US allies in the region since the start of the war.
Insisting Iran was the true victim of terrorism, Pezeshkian questioned why “Israel kills, yet Iran is subject to sanction”. He added: “They kill, we are sanctioned. Iran did not seek special treatment but wanted equal rights.”
Pezeshkian’s speech received domestic praise, but the hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, refused to describe the talks with the Americans as negotiations. He said: “Mr Araghchi [Iran’s foreign minister] has announced Iran’s conditions, and until Iran’s conditions are implemented, the strait of Hormuz will not be opened nor will there be any negotiation.”
He warned Iran’s neighbours implementing a US-induced ban on Iranian travel: “If you stand alongside the United States, we will not stand by and watch.” He cautioned that should Iranian flights face bans through regional cooperation with Washington, “their airports will have no flights either”.
Pezeshkian’s attendance at the UN’s signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear whether the US would issue a visa. Ultimately, Washington granted the permit but denied visas to several members of Pezeshkian’s entourage.
In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks had taken place between the two sides but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position.
He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.”
Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed.
Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours it said the strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.
It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control.
The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. The latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day.
The blockage in the strait is made worse by uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis – the Iran-backed Yemeni paramilitaries – of a second energy transport choke point, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean.
There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran, or indeed with the Houthis, as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular conflict that Americans think they are losing.
Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for it to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet.
Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears that Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.

articles.title_orig: Federal authorities investigating attorney, accountant linked to Epstein’s estate, source says
articles.title_zh: Federal authorities investigating attorney, accountant linked to Epstein’s estate, source says
articles.content_orig:
Federal authorities have opened an investigation into Jeffrey Epstein’s former attorney and accountant, a senior law enforcement official familiar with the probe told NBC News on Tuesday.
The lawyer, Darren Indyke, and the accountant, Richard Kahn, are administrators and executors of Epstein’s estate.
Interviews with witnesses have been ongoing, according to the law enforcement official, who could not confirm potential charges or allegations under review or a possible timeline for the case.
The Justice Department said in a statement that “we don’t comment on the existence, or lack thereof, of investigations. We have always said with regard to Epstein that if the evidence presents itself, we will investigate.”
Daniel Ruzumna, an attorney for Indyke and Kahn, said in a statement that the two had not been subpoenaed or asked to speak with federal prosecutors and have not been told they are the subjects or targets of any investigation. The focus and scope of the investigation were unclear, he said.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the probe.
Ruzumna said his clients are aware that federal prosecutors recently asked to speak with at least one person who “provided services” to Epstein.
He pointed to documents released in connection with the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which President Donald Trump signed last year, and said the documents showed that federal prosecutors did not consider Indyke and Kahn to be among Epstein’s potential co-conspirators during an investigation in 2018 and 2019.
Epstein died by suicide in 2019 at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York City, where he was jailed awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York, which had been in the process of prosecuting Epstein when he died and secured a conviction against accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, declined to comment.
Indyke and Kahn testified before the House Oversight Committee this year, Ruzumna said, and have given depositions in multiple lawsuits related to Epstein.
“Not a single individual has ever accused Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn of sexual abuse or trafficking, and they reject any suggestion that they were complicit in or in any way knowingly facilitated Mr. Epstein’s sexual abuse or trafficking — conduct that by all accounts occurred behind closed doors, in secluded locations, and at times when neither Mr. Indyke nor Mr. Kahn was present,” Ruzumna said.
Last week, the two men were named as defendants in their capacity as executors of his will in a lawsuit filed in federal court. Two women who say their photos were found in Epstein’s collection of sexually explicit images of children sued, saying they want Epstein’s estate to preserve and account for everything seized from his properties.
“We want a real, court-supervised process to identify and notify every survivor depicted in that collection,” said the attorney, Hillary Nappi. “Many of them have no idea their images exist in his files, and they deserve to know, and they deserve the chance to seek justice.”
An attorney for Indyke and Kahn said Wednesday that the lawsuit names them only in their capacity as co-executors of the Epstein estate, not as individuals.

articles.content_orig: By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/fbi-investigates-hackers-claim-to-have-stolen-employee-data-compromised-jobs-website Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter FBI investigates hackers' claim to have stolen employee data, compromised jobs website Nation Sep 23, 2026 5:37 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The FBI said Wednesday it was investigating a criminal hacking group's claims that it had stolen "very sensitive data" belonging to thousands of agents and applicants and that it had compromised the bureau's jobs website. "The FBI is aware of a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information," the FBI said in a statement. It said that while the "point of breach" was undetermined, "we are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk." WATCH: Patel explains why FBI no longer considers bestiality an automatic hiring disqualifier A message that circulated online from a hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for the hack. The jobs website, the main portal for prospective employees to learn about the FBI and initiate the application process, remained offline as of Wednesday afternoon. "We have compromised the FBI. We hold very sensitive data on almost ALL FBI Agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job," said the ShinyHunters message, which was directed to FBI Director Kash Patel and Brett Leatherman, the assistant director in charge of the bureau's cyber division. The claims could not immediately be verified. An email to an address associated with ShinyHunters was not immediately returned. In its message, ShinyHunters said it would give the bureau one week to correct or remove what it says are false allegations contained in an FBI public advisory from May that described the organization as a "cyber criminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion." That public service announcement characterized ShinyHunters as "threat actors" who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims," commonly harass or threaten victims and "may falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist." ShinyHunters said in its message to the FBI that it was "offended" by those characterizations and demanded that the FBI remove those claims. It did not say what would happen if the FBI did not do so within a week. "This is not a ransom, coercion, or extortion. Your federal policies do not apply here. This PSA is NOT financially motivated," the hacking group's message said. The FBI, the nation's premier federal law enforcement agency, has been a common hacking target. In March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating "suspicious activities" on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. Also that month, a pro-Iranian hacking group claimed to have hacked an account of Patel's and posted online what appear to be years-old photographs of him, along with a work resume and other personal documents dating back more than a decade. The FBI described the compromised information as "historical in nature" and said it involved "no government information." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. articles.title_orig: Acting Navy Secretary says eight sailors on USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide
articles.title_zh: Acting Navy Secretary says eight sailors on USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide
articles.content_orig:
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story contains discussion of suicide. Help is available if you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts or mental health matters. In the US, call or text 988 for help. The International Association for Suicide Prevention and Befrienders Worldwide have contact information for crisis centers around the world.
Eight US Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during a period that included when the ships undertook combat operations against Iran and the carrier set a modern record for its time at sea, according to a letter from the service’s acting secretary, which was obtained by CNN.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao revealed the number, which has not been previously reported and covers crew members from several ships that travel together, including the carrier, in written responses to questions posed by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand about the morale and mental health of the USS Abraham Lincoln’s crew. Cao wrote that no service members had killed themselves during the deployment.
The rate of suicide attempts among the Lincoln strike group’s sailors was roughly consistent with that of the entire active duty Navy in 2024, the most recent year for which the Pentagon has released suicide data. That year, the Navy saw 356 suicide attempts among its estimated 337,000 active duty sailors.
“Since the beginning of Lincoln’s deployment, there have been a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group,” Cao wrote to Gillibrand, a Democrat and member of the Senate Armed Services, in a letter dated Tuesday. “This number includes the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons.”
Between 6,000 and 7,000 US Navy sailors were deployed as part of the Lincoln strike group across roughly a half dozen ships — with the carrier kept out of port for over six months while conducting a high rate of combat operations against Iran.
“Eight attempted suicides is incredibly high,” one US military official told CNN, noting recent carrier strike group deployments have had one or two per year. “The strain of combat ops is much higher than normal deployments. No port calls, constant alerts, etc.”
The Navy did not respond ahead of publication to a request for comment about the letter.
“What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as ‘fake news’ turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members,” Gillibrand said in a statement Wednesday to CNN. “Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect. That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable.”
The Lincoln deployed with various mental health resources onboard, including five chaplains, one embedded integrated prevention counselor, one psychologist, one clinical social worker, three behavioral health technicians and one expeditionary facility dog, according to Cao’s letter.
CNN previously reported that two sailors assigned to the Lincoln strike group, one from the carrier and one from another ship, had jumped overboard in recent months. Both were rescued, US officials said. Others were prevented from jumping, according to reports from the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes.
In his letter to Gillibrand, Cao also confirmed that a sailor assigned to the airwing went overboard from the ship in early August but was “quickly recovered” and treated by the Lincoln’s medical department. “Additionally, one sailor attempted to go overboard in March and was stopped by his shipmates. That sailor was also provided immediate medical care and subsequently returned to homeport.”
The Navy previously said in a statement to CNN, “We have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship. We take every service member’s well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise.”
A US official also previously told CNN that the Navy does not believe there is a correlation between deployment length and thoughts of self-harm, and that man overboard incidents are not unique to this group.
A crew member serving on the Lincoln previously described to CNN that morale on the carrier was very low and said they had heard repeatedly about suicidal ideation by fellow crew members. And there were regular strains on essential amenities — toilets and water fountains around the ship frequently closed, and hot water was often unavailable, the crew member said.
“Everyday we wake up and listen to our captain speak, we are desperately hoping and anxious for updates on our return,” the crew member, speaking before the ship had been ordered to return to its home port in San Diego, told CNN. The ship left the Middle East in August and is expected back in San Diego in the coming weeks.
Other sailors aboard the Lincoln who spoke with CNN described conditions unlike their prior deployments, largely due to the combat that has kept the carrier from making stops at friendly ports. Ships can take on new supplies and allow their sailors to rest and relax during those port calls.
This story has been updated with additional details.
CNN’s Davis Winkie and Pamela Brown contributed to this report.
